finding.headline: Working past 65 with a plan to retire at 72 makes Social Security delay and Medicare timing the key rules here.
details: Social Security benefits rise for each month you delay past full retirement age, and the increase stops at age 70.

Medicare generally starts when you turn 65, and you have a 7-month Initial Enrollment Period around that date. If you miss it, you may pay a monthly late enrollment penalty that grows the longer you wait.
The 401(k) catch-up limit for ages 50 and over rises to $8,500 in 2027, so you can contribute up to $34,000 a year in your remaining working years.

details: Now, you pay about $3,928 in total tax on $41,000 of pay, so about $37,072 is left after tax.

finding.headline: Your savings should last in all 100 market scenarios we ran.
details: The spending goal of $46,000 a year lasted in 100 of 100 scenarios, and the basics were paid in 100 of 100. The most you could spend and stay safe in 90 of 100 scenarios is $54,600 a year.
We kept a simple plan: hold stocks at 110 minus your age, which is 44% now and 38% at retirement. At age 94, the middle outcome is $462,000 and the low outcome is $185,000.
Markets are uncertain, so these results are not promises. Your partner's survivor Social Security of $27,400 a year is also worth keeping in mind, and life cover of $410,000 is not in place.

finding.headline: You can count on $54,600 a year: $41,300 for basics and $13,300 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $41,300 a year.
Your spending goal is $46,000 a year, and it lasted in 100 of 100 scenarios, so the goal fits within what can be counted on.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Your spending now is about $26,028 a year more than your take-home pay, so until you retire the plan takes that from your savings each year. If that is wrong, change your spending now or your pay.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $33,100 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70 for each of you, which pays about $38,400 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $27,400 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 94. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
